documents.t: First-party auth, roles and their ceilings, workspace membership, cross-origin hardening and secret envelopes. # decision 0031 Auth in the api's domain: argon2id with fixed parameters, EdDSA access token from a derived key, refresh rotation with family revocation on reuse, lockout keyed on email (not id), and the single invariant that closes off enumeration 0032 The atomic Keycloak cutover: our own issuer in the guard without touching RBAC, /internal/* outside the JWT with a shared secret, web session in an httpOnly cookie with CSRF, and a migrated user indistinguishable from an email that doesn't exist 0037 The CORS the engine didn't have (/health returned 200 and the browser discarded it), its own plug instead of Corsica with /internal and /metrics outside the allowlist, WEB_ORIGIN read in a single place, and strictPort because the port is part of the CORS contract 0050 Credential always encrypted and saved; verification becomes a separate action. ADR 0004's gate (test BEFORE persisting) looked prudent and produced the worst outcome: a write-only field + refusal = a user with no credential AND no text to fix, because the screen never re-shows what they pasted. Storing and verifying are different questions, and tying them together made the second depend on the first having an answer right now. Applies to LLM and git alike — same table, same promise, and treating them differently would give two screens with distinct rules for the same object. The verdict has THREE states because the tester is a NO-OP on ollama/anthropic/openai: with a binary they'd return ok and the screen would claim a verification nobody ran (the ADR 0041 capability rule applied here). A bad key stops being an HTTP exception and becomes a 200 result, so the two @Catch that mapped it went away — a filter that can never fire is dead rule 0058 CSP locked down on the api, and project scope contained at the root. Revises item 7 of 0027, which had decided contentSecurityPolicy: false because "the api serves JSON and the CSP is the web's" — true, but not the point: the alternative to a GENERIC CSP isn't no header at all, it's a SPECIFIC CSP, and for something that only serves JSON the specific one is default-src 'none', which costs zero behavior. Two paths put the api's response outside the web's CSP reach: DIRECT navigation to a route (pasted link, redirect), rendered on the api's own origin, and frame-ancestors, which only applies to the framed document. Outside production the profile loosens only what the /docs Swagger UI needs, under the SAME condition that mounts Swagger — if it ever goes up in production, the CSP follows instead of silently blocking it. The options moved out of the main.ts literal into security-headers.ts for the same reason that already moved cors-origins.ts: at boot they weren't testable, and the proof has to be a real request, because false and a directives object are both "valid config" and only differ in the HTTP response. Along with it comes containing projectId: it arrives from the route parameter already percent-decoded by Express, so ..%2F..%2Fetc became ../../etc and escaped the root — hitting not just reading and WRITING permissions.json but also the scope that AUTHORIZES the terminal via 0055, i.e., the policy pointing at the wrong place. Validation lives where the root is derived, not in each caller, for the same reason the function exists: duplicated checking is checking that one day diverges. Also records the seven CodeQL dismissals with the reason for each — among them js/insufficient-password-hash over an OAuth state HMAC, where there's no password and a slow hash would be a mistake 0059 The key that signs the git OAuth state has no default. Born from one of 0058's dismissals: dismissing js/insufficient-password-hash was right — there's no password there, the "password" is GIT_OAUTH_STATE_SECRET, a server-side HMAC key, and HMAC-SHA256 is the right primitive. What the argument didn't consider is that a server key with a known default value signs nothing, and that was the case: both read points did process.env.GIT_OAUTH_STATE_SECRET ?? 'dev-oauth-state-secret-change-me'. The same failure mode WEB_ORIGIN had already had closed in cors-origins.ts, and worse for two reasons — the value is PUBLIC (it's in the .env.example of an open-source repo, not a weak default, a published secret), and what it protects is the state, the only obstacle to forging the callback of a route that needs to be public: with the key known, anyone can sign {projectId, userId, provider} of their choice and make the callback write, into that payload's project, the git token obtained from the provider. The detail that decides the shape of the fix is that docker-compose.prod.yml supplied the literal as a fallback, so on the REAL error path the variable WAS defined — requiring just "not empty" wouldn't have caught anything, and that's why the example literal is rejected explicitly, along with a 16-character floor that turns the configuration table's ever-present "weak = CSRF" into an actual check. The check runs at BOOT, not on first use: an api that only failed when someone tried to connect git would stand for weeks accepting a state signed with a public key. Resolved into a single function for the RN-092 reason — there were two copies of the same literal, and diverging them would make the callback reject every legitimate state. Deliberate breakage: production with no variable set stops booting, which is the goal and not a side effect. The four sibling secrets of the same compose (AUTH_JWT_SECRET, BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN, CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY, SECRET_KEY_BASE) were left declaredly out, in the backlog — closed later by the same rule, with no new ADR, in RN-114 0084 Social login (GitHub/GitLab), revising the backlog from ADRs 0031/0032 — the ban lifted only for this piece, by the product owner's explicit decision. SocialLoginCallbackUseCase ends by calling the SAME EmitirSessaoUseCase as password login — no second session format. The OAuth client is reused (GithubOauthClient/GitlabOauthClient gain buildLoginAuthorizeUrl/fetchIdentity), but the state is NOT: domain/auth/social-oauth-state.ts signs with the SAME GIT_OAUTH_STATE_SECRET key only because the payload is structurally incompatible — a purpose: 'social_login' discriminant checked BEFORE any other field is what keeps a state from git's CONNECTION flow from being accepted here (RN-273), which would be privilege escalation. New social_identities table (migration 0047), keyed by (provider, provider_user_id) — never email/login, which can change owner (RN-276). The callback decides in three steps: identity already known → log in; email matches an existing account AND is provider-verified → link, and while at it verify the account's email if it wasn't already (RN-279); email matches but NOT verified → refuse, account takeover (RN-274); no matching account → provision a NEW passwordless user, reusing the same "pending" state from the Keycloak migration (RN-278) — here the email doesn't need to be verified, because there's no account to protect (RN-275). Reuses the SAME OAuth app as the git connection flow — zero new environment variables —, changing only redirect_uri and scope (minimal, no repo/api) per request; the OPERATOR action of registering the second callback with the provider is what justifies the breaking/ branch. The access token never travels in the URL: session cookies are written in the callback, and the web boot already rebuilds the session on its own 0096 Real SMTP in MailSender, closing the backlog item open since 0032 ("real SMTP stays future config"). nodemailer over plain SMTP transport — a stateful LINE protocol with MIME/STARTTLS/AUTH, unlike the JSON HTTP APIs the rest of the product integrates — behind MAIL_TRANSPORT (log, default including in production, or smtp), selected by a useFactory in AuthUseCasesModule without touching any use case. SMTP_HOST/SMTP_USER/SMTP_PASSWORD/SMTP_FROM follow the RN-114 pattern in production when the mode is smtp, but WITHOUT the public default the four original RN-114 variables had — the bar only kicks in once the operator opts into smtp, validated in SmtpMailSender's constructor (exercised by the useFactory when the provider graph is assembled, same design as CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY), not by an eager call in main.ts. Plain-text body, never HTML — the port carries no structure for rich bodies. Investigation found a real gap before implementing: email_verification had no web route at all (verificarEmail existed in apps/web/src/lib/auth.ts with no caller) — /verificar-email (VerifyEmailPage.tsx) closes that, mirroring SetPasswordPage.tsx 0127 ResolveEffectiveRoleUseCase.forProject stays projectRole ?? workspaceRole — the project row OVERRIDES the workspace one in BOTH directions, and restricting someone on a sensitive project (workspace developer → project viewer) is a deliberate capability that "the higher of the two" would delete. What lands instead are TWO caps on the write path, refused with 403 and configurable nowhere: nobody downgrades a workspace owner (so a maintainer can no longer lock the owner out of their own project), and nobody downgrades THEMSELVES (undoing needs the very role being given up). The owner is read from workspace_members.role, never workspaces.created_by — created_by is a historical fact that appears in no authorization path, and a cap reading it would shield a creator who already transferred ownership while leaving the current owner exposed. Cap 2 is stated WITHOUT a threshold ("yourself", not "below maintainer"): the threshold version copies a number out of a controller's @RequireRole into the domain and ages silently if the route's minimum changes; the declared price is that an owner demoting themselves to maintainer — reversible — also falls. They live in the USE CASE with the rule in domain/iam/tetos-de-rebaixamento.ts, not in RolesGuard, which authorizes the CALLER against the route and sees neither body (dto.role) nor target; the FORM follows domain/actions/decide.ts (RN-154/RN-418) minus its outcome, since a synchronous human call has no approval queue to fall into. The three OpenAPI descriptions RN-471 declared false ("the higher of this one and what the person already has", "includes whoever inherits access from the workspace") are corrected here. Declared still possible: downgrading another maintainer, self-PROMOTION (unchanged, not opened here), the workspace-level POST which has no cap at all, and self-downgrade through REMOVAL — RemoveProjectMemberUseCase gained no cap, and the premise that removal is always benign is FALSE (it is, when the workspace role catches the fall; it is irreversible self-downgrade when it doesn't). Both removal cases are pinned in tests, the open one included. The web stays out on purpose and for a structural reason: the screen can compute cap 2 but NOT cap 1, since listProjectMembers returns the project-row role and the target's workspace role is out of the client's reach — half a gate would be the second source of role RN-471 warns against; meanwhile the refusal shows, via the mensagemDaApi toast #444 added 0156 The self-downgrade cap reaches the OTHER door: removing your own project_members row. ADR 0127 capped only the write path and left this movement out in writing, pinning it in a test whose name documented the hole — "removal STILL gets to downgrade whoever called it" — and predicting the cost of closing it (RemoveProjectMemberUseCase.execute's signature). This is that next person. Removal does not delete a role, it SWAPS the effective one: projectRole ?? workspaceRole (RN-471) starts resolving through the second term, so a maintainer whose authority came from the project row, viewer in the workspace, dropped to viewer with no way back — restoring is POST :projectId/members, which demands the very maintainer just abandoned; with no workspace role at all, the fall is to NO access. The rule is cap 2, not a new cap: ehAutoRebaixamento compares effective-today against effective-after and never needed to know which route the second arrived by, so remocaoEhAutoRebaixamento DELEGATES to it passing the workspace role as the requested one, reimplementing no comparison. It exists as its own function for the single case the other's signature cannot state — an actor with no workspace role, where "after" is nothing, which is not a Role. Cap 1 gets no counterpart, on purpose: owner is the top of ROLE_ORDER, so removing a workspace owner's project row can only RAISE their effective role — it is in fact the only way to undo the restriction cap 1 forbids creating, and a cap there would refuse only benign movements while making permanent the state ADR 0127 was born to eliminate. Stated without a threshold, like cap 2, and the declared price rides along: self-removal from project owner down to workspace maintainer is reversible and falls too — the one benign movement that used to pass and now refuses. The message is its OWN, because whoever clicked "remove" asked for no role change and deserves the mechanism, not the add phrase. Refuses: an owner cap on removal, a second comparison rule, touching forProject, extending to the workspace scope (whose POST still has no cap and whose member @Delete does not exist), blocking removal of OTHER people who drop, and a client-side gate — MembersSection.handleRemove already surfaces mensagemDaApi in a toast, and computing only the half the screen can compute is the half-gate ADR 0127 refused. Closes BRB-001 0157 The self-movement cap reaches the WORKSPACE upsert, and self-PROMOTION — which ADR 0127 left standing in writing — becomes a breach and closes. AddWorkspaceMemberUseCase was a twelve-line passthrough that never received the actor, on a route requiring owner: the same class of defect as project_members, one scope up and worse, because here there is no level above to catch the fall and no member @Delete at all (measured; ADR 0156 had used the same fact to postpone this). An owner writing themselves viewer lost the whole workspace — every project, the LLM spend that is theirs by RN-060, and the very ability to invite whoever would restore them — with undoing being this same route, demanding the owner just abandoned. The cap does not count owners, by the literal criterion of ADR 0127 ("stated as a clause, it has no number to age"): a count adds a read that can fall out of step with the write, must judge whether a second owner who left the company still counts, and makes the same request with the same body pass today and refuse tomorrow. The stronger argument is that the clause already produces the invariant a count would exist to guarantee — a workspace never ends up with zero owners, because removing the last one would require that owner to do it, which is exactly the refused movement. Cap 1 gets no counterpart here, and it was considered rather than mirrored: unlike removal (ADR 0156), the movement DOES exist — an owner can demote another owner. It is refused because cap 1 is a rule about hierarchy inversion, and @RequireRole('owner') already makes inversion impossible in this scope: whoever can call is never below whoever they touch. Adding it, on top of the missing removal route, would make owner an absorbing state nobody leaves over HTTP — offboarding, ownership rotation and fixing a wrong invite would all need direct database writes, which is the class of state ADR 0127 was born to eliminate, rebuilt with the sign flipped. So demoting another owner STAYS, reversible through the same route by any remaining owner. Self-promotion closes on both association routes. ADR 0127 had recorded it as a capability that stayed ("the caps are about going down"); reopened here, the answer is that both halves are one movement — a person deciding alone what authority they hold — and the upward half is the only one that ESCALATES privilege, which is precisely what that ADR could claim its caps never did. Rewriting the SAME role still passes: an idempotent upsert is not a movement, and refusing it would break seed.ts. The comparison is not copied: it becomes one classifier, autoMovimentoDoProprioPapel, returning the SENSE rather than a boolean, because the caller needs it to pick the message. ehAutoRebaixamento survives as a reading of that classifier — on purpose, not for compatibility: remocaoEhAutoRebaixamento delegates to it, and widening it would make REMOVAL refuse self-promotion too, breaking the benign movement ADR 0156 protected by name. Four messages, one per sense and per scope — nobody who tried to promote themselves reads the downgrade phrase, and nobody capped in the workspace is told to ask a maintainer. Refuses: counting owners, an owner cap in this scope, creating a workspace member @Delete (a new door would need this same cap plus the last-owner judgement), widening the removal door, touching forProject for the third ADR running, and a client gate — there is none to build, since no apps/web caller of this route exists. Declared cost: a legitimate maintainer who needs owner now depends on someone else. Closes BRB-002 0158 The envelope starts saying WHICH master key wrapped it, and that label never decides whether it opens. The runbook's own page states the hole ("The wrapped_dek stored in the database doesn't identify which key wrapped it"), and two defects follow: the middle step of rotation has no progress — whoever interrupts it cannot tell where it stopped, and "is anything still on the old key?" has no SQL answer, only re-running the script for its printed counter — and a wrong key and a corrupt blob land in the same catch, two diagnoses with opposite actions wearing one generic failure. So both envelope tables gain a nullable key_id, always together, since they share the envelope and the script and changing one would leave an estate where the query answers half. The value is the key's fingerprint, HMAC-SHA256(derived key, label) truncated — which answers the open question the activity left ("not a hash of the key, that gives whoever reads the database an offline verification oracle") by measuring rather than assuming: the envelope is AES-256-GCM, which AUTHENTICATES, so testing a candidate passphrase against wrapped_dek was ALREADY a perfect oracle costing one scrypt; testing it against the fingerprint costs the same scrypt. No oracle is created, and no variable is added either — the operator types the fingerprint nowhere, it is a pure function of the key already published, which is what makes the old "one more metadatum to keep in sync" objection true of an arbitrary id and false of a fingerprint. The label is observability, never authority, and that is where this decision departs from the obvious one: decrypt stays byte for byte, and rewrap still decides "already on the current key" by ATTEMPTING. Using the label to skip the attempt was considered and refused for a failure mode of its own — a row labelled "current" whose envelope sits on the old key would be silently skipped, stay out of the re-wrapped count, and step 3 would make it unreadable forever, turning a metadata inconsistency into secret loss. So the label serves three things outside the crypto decision: the progress query (IS DISTINCT FROM, never <>, so NULL counts as pending), the diagnosis when NEITHER key opens, and the stamp rewrap writes beside the new envelope. No back-fill: key_id is born on the next write, existing rows stay NULL meaning "written before this column" and never "on the current key" — with the declared cost that on an existing installation the query only starts meaning something after the first rotation. The api prints the current fingerprint at boot, because a column nobody can compare against anything is useless. Refuses: KMS/HSM/per-tenant keys (ADR 0027 stands), an index on key_id, and moving the diagnosis into the hot read path 0173 Workspace member removal is born, capped by the SAME clause. DELETE /workspaces/:workspaceId/members/:userId (owner, 204) ends offboarding by database write, which ADR 0157 refused to open in passing. Cap 2 is inherited with no new rule — remocaoEhAutoRebaixamento with the workspace role as today's effective role and none as the role after, since nothing above catches the fall — so removing YOURSELF is always 403, and that same clause protects the last owner without counting: only an owner calls the route and nobody removes themselves, so every removal leaves at least the caller. Removing ANOTHER owner is allowed; cap 1 still has no counterpart. The removal cascades in one transaction (the target's project_members rows in the workspace, their project device keys and PATs there) and then drops their live runner per project through the RN-520 path. Declared open: workspaces.created_by does not change, so removing the creator leaves agents spending the creator's LLM key (RN-058).

documents.t: The provider contract, the model catalog and curation, model bindings, metering and budgets. # decision 0040 The dashboard card and the summary line show only USD (the prices' currency of origin, with no conversion involved) — a divergence isolated to this surface, TokenMeter default/live remain in R$+US$; per-workspace currency preference with a manual rate is recorded and deferred 0041 OpenAI-compatible base over node:http (not the SDK, to get an INACTIVITY timeout), error normalized with a mandatory code in the chunk, capabilities in two layers with agent binding refused without native tool calling, and a contract suite where the contract owns the assertions and the harness owns the dialect 0042 Catalog sync by capability, with a discovered model entering disabled and a vanished model marked instead of deleted; two independent availability axes (owner curation × remote reality); a cascade that revalidates capability when it drops a level; and price frozen in token_usage so old cost stays reproducible, with append-only auditing outside the outbox 0043 The six 9b providers (NVIDIA NIM, Together, DeepInfra, Bitdeer, Vultr, OpenRouter) enter as config over the base, each investigated from scratch against the official docs — capability declared only when proven, with two real cases of a decision reverted live during implementation; the only new hook in the base is the parseErrorFrame that only OpenRouter (the hub) needed 0049 Model curation per workspace: models.is_active was a column for the WHOLE installation — a workspace A owner turning on a model turned it on for B too, with the spend landing in the budget of whoever didn't decide. The catalog stays global because name, price and capabilities are facts about the provider, and duplicating it per workspace would create N truths about the same model besides splitting token_usage.model_id; only the decision migrates, to workspace_models. Absence of a row IS the off state — there's no third state, and that's how RN-043 survives with no column the sync could ever run over; turning off is an UPDATE, not a DELETE, so as not to erase who decided together. The picker's route hangs off the PROJECT (the three screens that consume it already had projectId, none had workspace), and isActive leaves the Model entity: whoever needs it uses a type that only exists with a workspace in hand 0051 Capability facets read from the provider, and "what it's for" as workspace curation. Sync never queried the remote for modality (supportsVision: local?.supportsVision ?? false), so the column was born false and died false — the 338 models from OpenRouter's first real sync all came out with no vision, including the 181 the provider declares multimodal. Image input and output become DISTINCT axes: reading a diagram and drawing one solve different problems. The other half of the request — "best for code/documentation" — doesn't exist in any catalog, and deriving it from the model's name would be a guess dressed up as data (ADR 0041); so it's the operator's opinion and lives in workspace_models, like all curation since ADR 0049. The two axes don't mix: marking a use doesn't turn the model on (the is_active column has DEFAULT true, and the new row is born with false explicit), and the screen never writes "doesn't read images", because false there means "the provider didn't declare it". Video was left out: zero models across nine providers, a filter that would never match anything 0063 Two audiences for the same spend: the owner's bill and the member's consumption. The request was a spend summary tab in the spirit of OpenRouter's activity, and the data was never the problem — token_usage has provider, model, actor, tokens and price FROZEN since 0042; what was missing was the AGGREGATIONS (there was none by model, by project within the workspace, by session or by person). The difficulty is the collision between two existing rules: by RN-058 the key the agent spends is the OWNER's, and by RN-060 that key's bill is his and only his — so "how much did I spend" is, literally, asking for a slice of someone else's bill. The two easy outs are both wrong: opening the credential report filtered revokes RN-060 through the back door (the answer would still talk about provider and key, and summing the lines reconstructs the bill), and showing nothing leaves the one person forbidden from seeing the consumption being exactly the one who is it. The decision separates the QUESTIONS: the owner's is by CREDENTIAL (provider, key, bill) and still requires owner, reused whole instead of rewritten; the member's is by ACTOR, in tokens and estimated cost, WITHOUT breaking down by provider or credential. The actor comes from the authenticated token and there's no parameter to write someone else's id into — "a member doesn't see another actor's line" becomes a property of the signature, not a check someone might forget; proven by test, and the mutation that removes the filter kills it. The provider axis DOESN'T EXIST in the new aggregation (sumGroupedBy has model/project/actor/session/day and nothing else): the absence is what keeps the member's view from getting it by accident, and for the same reason two providers serving a model with the same name fall into a single line. Agent doesn't enter the member's account because token_usage records who spent, not who ordered the spend. No charting library — two shapes, one series each, an inline <rect> handles it —, and the daily series comes DENSE from the api, otherwise three calls across three weeks turn into three sticking-together bars. No migration: measured at 525 thousand rows, the queries come out at 55 ms and 38 ms per seq scan, and an index on created_at would bring them to 32 ms and 19 ms — the gain is recorded and the index comes later 0064 Area scope in the model cascade, and the global agent binding. The request: area leads and their subgroup sharing a current model, with the agent free to diverge — an inheritable pattern, a decision the user had already made. The cascade (session > agent > project > workspace) gained area between agent and project, and answering WHERE it goes surfaced an inconsistency that needed a decision before coding: the agent binding was GLOBAL (scope_id = plain slug, the route's :projectId deliberately IGNORED since Phase 9a) and area is PER PROJECT since ADR 0053 — a per-project scope ABOVE a global scope would make the same agent resolve different models only where an area existed, behavior dependent on a data accident. Two mutually exclusive outs: make the agent binding per-project (changes existing behavior), or put area BELOW agent (contradicts "inheritable pattern", because almost every binding today IS of an agent). The first was chosen: agent and area's scope_id became COMPOSITE — `:<slug 0075 Embeddings in the LLMProvider contract. The Chat RAG that's coming needs vectors, and the product didn't know how to make them: the word "embedding" appeared in ONE comment, in bitdeer-provider.ts's prose. The operation enters as embed?, optional under the same two-sided contract as listModels (whoever declares the capability implements it; whoever doesn't declare doesn't expose it), in BATCHES because an index receives N chunks at once — and from that comes the most important guarantee: one vector per input or an error, never a shorter list, because order is the only link between input and vector and a partial response is undetectable afterward. The error THROWS normalized by code instead of turning into a chunk, with 0041's taxonomy untouched: the chunk's reason is preserving spend from a turn in progress, and there's nothing to preserve here. The return states dimensions checked against what CAME BACK (not copied from the catalog — a vector index has a fixed dimension), the model the provider said it used (an alias resolves to a dated version, and that's what goes to metering for the frozen-price reason, RN-044) and inputTokens/estimated with RN-041's distinction. The capability is in TWO layers as 0041 required, but with a difference that had to be named: tool calling is a gradient (a model with no tool still converses) and embedding is EXCLUSION — nomic-embed-text doesn't answer questions and llama3.2 doesn't return vectors, two disjoint sets, and that's why the question didn't fit any existing supports_* column. Provider: capabilities.embeddings, MANDATORY by the same argument that made code mandatory. Model: supportsEmbeddings/embeddingDimensions in the catalog, optional because absence means "the provider didn't say" — Ollama is the only one of the nine that publishes this per model (capabilities: ["embedding"] in /api/tags). Only ollama declares true, proven by EXECUTION against the real 0.32.1 daemon (2 inputs → 2 vectors of 768, prompt_eval_count: 10), an execution that also produced the test for the 501 a chat model returns. The other eight stay false: seven for lack of proof (no key in the environment, and the only paid smoke test that has ever run was for CHAT — on a hub, embedding routes to a different provider), and Anthropic for lacking the operation (their docs say to use a third party). The base's dialect is proven separately, with the contract suite running a second time against it with the capability turned on, and that's what makes it cheap to turn a provider on once the key exists. Two declared cuts: embedding metering doesn't exist yet because token_usage.session_id is NOT NULL and indexing a repository doesn't happen inside a session, and the models.supports_embeddings column waited for another wave's migration slot 0076 provider becomes a spend dimension again, and containment shifts to the TYPE. Revises 0063, which had excluded the axis with a no-middle-ground sentence ("the absence is structural… there's no argument to pass") — the argument is still right, and that's exactly why the reopening, decided by the product owner, comes with the containment written in. What 0063 didn't separate and usage asked for: the owner couldn't see, WITHIN the sliding window, where the money went (credential-spend answers by provider, but in calendar months and tied to the key that exists today), and person and agent showed up in the same ranking. sumGroupedBy gains provider, the owner's report gains porProvider (RN-186), and the member gains no field at all. Containment changes FORM, not strength: there are two overloads, and the scope that carries actor — the only one the member's view has — only accepts SpendDimensionDoAtor, which is Exclude<SpendDimension, 'provider'>; asking for provider with actor DOESN'T COMPILE (RN-187). No if on the combination, on purpose, for the same reason auto mode's resolution lives in the repository and not in decide.ts (RN-153/154): a dynamic check suggests a dynamic guarantee, and that's what the next refactor removes without leaving a red test. Exclude instead of a second hand-written list, because a parallel restricted list ages silently. Person and agent become porOwner/porAgente, a PARTITION of porAtor in the use case rather than two queries (RN-188) — 0063 measured that the cost grows with the size of token_usage, not with the request's. The index on token_usage(created_at) that 0063 measured and deferred enters here (migration 0044): 55 ms → 32 ms and 38 ms → 19 ms at 525 thousand rows. Consequence declared without softening: the guarantee went from "impossible to express" to "impossible to compile", which is weaker — what holds the price down are two independent barriers, and the other is the member's route having no dimension parameter at all, with @ts-expect-error covering the first (if the barrier falls, tsc fails on the UNUSED directive, instead of the test passing while testing nothing). The SCREEN is left out, declared 0077 Model ranking by capability, with no invented score. The handoff asked for a "best models by capability" table with a SCORE per capability (code 9.4, image 9.1…) and an ideal badge on ModelPicker "when the model covers all capabilities the agent requires". The investigation found both requests need the same data the product doesn't have: the score is FICTIONAL, from the mock (no provider publishes "code quality", no product metric measures that), and "capabilities required per agent" doesn't exist in the domain — ModelsSection itself had already renamed the "Agent · capabilities" column to just "Agent" for that reason, and promising it again would reopen a gap that had already been refused. A second, structural barrier closes off the badge on its own: the agent-binding ModelPicker reads GET /projects/:id/models (role viewer), and curation (uses, ADR 0051) only exists in ModelComCuradoria, from a maintainer-only route — linking the two would widen RBAC, a separate product decision. The badge is NOT built (documented in ModelPicker.tsx itself); the ranking table IS built, with two REAL signals: "recommended"/"alternative" come from the curation (uses) the workspace already marked, ordered by how many agents IN THIS PROJECT already resolve to that model via the cascade (the most honest signal without inventing a score), cost as a tiebreaker; a capability with no curated coverage shows the gap, never hides the row 0110 Closes the "budget per area" backlog item open since Phase 8. agent_areas gains budget_micros/spent_micros, mirroring max_parallel on the SAME row — no new table, and not the generic budgets table (its CHECK enforces exactly one of project/session, built for a two-way exclusion, not a third scope). It's a THIRD ceiling ADDITIVE to project/session budgets, checked and incremented independently by CheckBudgetGateUseCase/RecordLlmUsageUseCase — explicitly NOT the ADR 0064 model-binding cascade, which the two mechanisms share only a name with. spent_micros accumulates whenever the actor belongs to an area (resolved by the pure areaDo, no DB hit for an actor with none), with or without a cap set; SetAreaBudgetUseCase requires maintainer and accepts null to clear the cap 0114 Native Ollama detection in pnpm dev's bootstrap: preflight.mjs confirms by HTTP that whatever holds OLLAMA_PORT (default 11434, the same default a native install uses) really is an Ollama daemon, asks ONCE whether to reuse it (defaulting to yes with no TTY, since the menu runs commands with stdin from /dev/null on purpose), and persists the answer to .env (OLLAMA_MODE=host|container) via escreverEnv — the first thing in the repo that WRITES .env in place rather than only reading it. ollama/ollama-model-loader move behind profiles: ["local-llm"], toggled per command by scripts/dev/perfil-ollama.sh; a profiled service invisible to docker compose config by default forced detectarOllamaNativo to grow its own conflict-reporting path (the generic per-port loop would otherwise stop seeing a genuine non-Ollama occupant) and forced api's depends_on: ollama to be removed (Compose refuses the whole file when a service outside an inactive profile depends on one inside it). New "Docker › Reconfigurar Ollama" menu item forgets the decision, on demand 0115 Hugging Face model pull gets its OWN small table, huggingface_model_pull_requests, never proposed_actions — traced and rejected because that pipeline's session_id NOT NULL, its decide()/agent_autonomy policy resolution, and its closed ActionType vocabulary are all built around an AGENT being supervised by a human, and here the actor already IS the human, gated by role on the route, with no session and no agent in play. The two-step confirmation IS the pending_confirmation → confirmed transition, not an extra flag — ConfirmModelPullUseCase refuses (409) to run it twice, and only a successful confirm calls OllamaProvider.pullModel SYNCHRONOUSLY inside the request (the api has no background-job runner of its own; GET .../pull-requests/:id exists for callers unwilling to hold that connection open). repoId travels in the request body, not the route, because the Hub's <publisher>/<model> shape breaks single-segment path matching (same fix already used for file paths in code.controller.ts). A hand-curated, case-sensitive allowlist of official Hub publishers (ADR 0042's "manual curation always," applied to a new badge) gates the default search results; community results require an explicit, off-by-default opt-in paired with a persistent security warning 0166 The hub's routing preference lives in the model binding, travels with it, and is frozen in metering. Measured on a v6.1.0 install (AT-090): 23 of 24 calls of one model through OpenRouter were served by an upstream roughly four times slower, because the request body never said how to choose (provider.sort). Decided by the maintainer: model_bindings.routing_preference (`price 0188 The REAL cost the provider returns becomes the metering number (AT-270, owner decision 30/09): when the response carries it (OpenRouter's usage.cost), it is token_usage.cost_micros, what the turn returns to the engine, what the budgets add and what the Spend tab shows; the frozen catalog price (ADR 0042) stays the number only where the response says nothing. The row's price becomes IMPLICIT (cost ÷ tokens, flagged price_implicit, the same column and function as ADR 0179's Jev), what the catalog would have charged goes alongside in catalog_cost_micros, and the resolved model and gen-… id are recorded. estimated keeps meaning the TOKENS; BYOK falls back to the catalog. The same round records the PARTS the dialect reports — cached_input_tokens and reasoning_tokens (AT-272), never added to the totals, null meaning "didn't say" — and medir-execucao.ts reports how much of the input was cache read 0198 The SEMANTIC duplicate of a story or business rule is WARNED by embedding with a threshold, never refused (AT-171, owner decision 01/10): after the item is written, its title is compared with the project's titles of the same kind through the RAG's RagEmbeddingService, and a cosine at or above 0.80 — a STARTING POINT, not calibrated, because the environment could not record real vectors — returns a warning to the agent in the tool result and backlog.semantic_duplicate_warned in the log. Without an embedding provider the check is SKIPPED and says why. Its spend is metered as its own token_usage row (actor system/duplicata-semantica) — ONE exception to ADR 0075's cut, which still holds for indexing and search. The exact duplicate is still refused (RN-080/081)
