It survives for a behavioral reason and not a compatibility one: whoever delegates to it is remocaoEhAutoRebaixamento, and REMOVAL only sees the lower half. Widening it would make removal also refuse self-promotion — and removing one's own project row that restricted someone is precisely how one undoes the restriction ceiling 1 prevents from being created, the benign move point 3 of ADR 0156 protected explicitly. Unifying everything would have changed, in passing, a door this ADR did not open. 6. The messages are specific by DIRECTION and by SCOPE. There are four, and none serves two things: whoever tried to promote themselves does not receive the downgrade sentence (it is not what they did), and whoever hits the workspace ceiling is not sent to talk to a maintainer — there the role that undoes is owner. It is the same discipline as point 5 of ADR 0156 and of RN-470: do not collapse two states because they share an outcome. 7. The actor's role comes from the repository, not from ResolveEffectiveRoleUseCase. It is the inverse of 0156's choice, for the same reason it gave ("no extra dependency for one read"): in the project use cases ResolveEffectiveRoleUseCase enters so the actor's role does not become a second composition of projectRole ?? workspaceRole written by hand; in the workspace there is no composition to protect — forWorkspace IS workspaces.findMemberRole —, and this use case already has the repository in hand, because it is with it that it writes. 8. 403, in the use case, never in RolesGuard. Nothing new: the guard authorizes the CALLER against the route's @RequireRole and sees neither the body (dto.role) nor the target (dto.userId), and this ceiling is about the actor↔target relation. The whole reasoning is in ADR 0127 and is not repeated here. 9. Promotion is enforced even though it is unreachable over HTTP on this route. With @RequireRole('owner'), the actor is already at the top and there is nowhere to go up — the upper half of the ceiling, in the workspace scope, is a mechanism that does not fire today. It enters anyway, and tested, for the reason ceiling 2 always had not to have a threshold: the use case does not presume the guard, and it is what stays right the day the route changes its minimum. It is the same design as the capability refusal of RN-514, implemented and tested before having a trigger.
documents.s: Decision

documents.t: Counting owners. See point 2. Neither "only the last one", nor "only if no other active owner remains". The clause has no number to age, and already produces the invariant of never having zero owners. A workspace owner ceiling in this scope. See point 3. It is neither a forgotten symmetry nor a reflexive discard: it is a rule about hierarchy inversion on a route where inversion is impossible, and adding it would make owner a state nobody leaves over HTTP. A workspace member removal route. Its absence is part of this ADR's context (it is why self-downgrade has no way back), and creating it would be opening a new door while closing another — and the new door would be born needing the same ceiling, plus the judgment about removing the last owner, which this ADR does not have the material to make. A separate decision, if someone asks for it. Widening the project member REMOVAL ceiling to promotion. See point 5. ADR 0156 protected that move in writing and it stays byte for byte. Touching ResolveEffectiveRoleUseCase.forProject. Third ADR in a row in which this is said: projectRole ?? workspaceRole stays in both directions. A gate on the screen. There is no screen: POST /workspaces/:workspaceId/members has no caller in apps/web — measured; the only occurrence is the generated type in api-types.generated.ts. Whoever calls the route today is seed.ts (through the use case, with the owner as actor) and direct integrations. There is no toast to adjust, and no web line changes.
documents.s: What this ADR explicitly rejects

documents.t: A legitimate maintainer who needs owner in the project now depends on another person. It is the direct cost of the decision of point 4, and it is not hypothetical: it was the path through which someone with the route's role gave themselves the role they needed for the next task. It remains reachable — by any other maintainer of the project, and by any owner of the workspace —, and what is bought is that role elevation now takes two people. It is the same trade ADR 0127 made for going down, with the same price in the same currency. ADR 0127's sentence about self-promotion becomes FALSE, and it is this ADR that replaces it. It remains written there, like every superseded decision in this repository; whoever reads it has to get here. That is why the index line and the docblock of ehAutoRebaixamento name the revision. The test that pinned the permission was INVERTED, not deleted, with its name keeping the origin — "raising one's own role was allowed for being 'not a downgrade', and becomes 403 (ADR 0157)". The same form 0156 used for the removal gap test. It is the evidence of why the capability existed, and it is not thrown away. One more query per workspace association, and only one: the actor's role. The route is an administration one and the comparison is pure, so the cost is the same 0127 accepted in the project (where there were two) and 0156 on removal (two). The signature changed, and there were TWO callers — the controller and apps/api/src/db/seed.ts, which passes owner.id as the actor. There the actor and the target are different people on purpose, so no ceiling is reached and the seed gains no exception at all. CreateWorkspaceUseCase is not a caller, and it is good that it is not: it writes the creator as owner through the repository, inside the creation transaction, which is a legitimate self-promotion — the only one in the product — and would come to be refused if it were ever routed through here. The comment next to the null-role clause records this. The route's surface changed without changing any success response, and it is in docs/security-surface.md: role:owner remains in the table and remains what RolesGuard enforces, but it is no longer the complete answer to "who can do what here" — the third route in this family to receive that note. Still possible, by name: an owner downgrading ANOTHER owner (point 3, reversible through the same route); downgrading anyone who is not the caller, in any scope, which is the usual capability; and self-PROMOTION through the removal of one's own project row — removing the row that restricted someone raises their effective role, and ADR 0156 protected that move on purpose.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. It corresponds to BRB-016 of the maintainer's register, which declares a dependency on BRB-010 — and the dependency is literal: this decision changes the envelope format, and the proof that the current format survives a whole rotation was born in the same delivery, in RN-562, before this line of code. It does not revoke ADR 0027: the envelope scheme, CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY_PREVIOUS and rewrap-deks.ts remain as they are.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: CREDENTIALS_MASTER_KEY wraps the DEKs that encrypt the user's secrets — LLM keys in user_credentials and git tokens in project_git_connections. Its rotation is the procedure with the worst outcome in the runbook, and the runbook itself writes why (docs/runbook.md, section "What's at stake"): "The wrapped_dek stored in the database doesn't identify which key wrapped it." Measured on 2026-09-12, in the checkout: file:line what is there apps/api/src/db/schema/llm.ts:255 wrappedDek: text('wrapped_dek').notNull() — six envelope columns, none saying which key apps/api/src/db/schema/git.ts:72 idem, the SAME six columns envelope-encryption.service.ts:128-138 decrypt tries the current one and falls back to the previous one, inside a catch that does not distinguish the reason envelope-encryption.service.ts:148-160 rewrap does the same, and the catch without a reason is what decides whether the record is already on the current key docs/runbook.md, "Before: size it up" the only possible query counts total rows per table — never how many are left Two concrete defects come out of this: Step 2 of the rotation has no progress. Whoever interrupts the script midway does not know where it stopped; the only way to find out is to run it again and read the count it prints. And the question that decides step 3 — "is there still a credential on the old key?" — has no answer in SQL. Wrong key and corrupted blob are the same catch. Both produce the same generic failure, and they are diagnoses with opposite actions: one asks to republish the previous key, the other asks to investigate the record. The lesson that governs this area is RN-475: an id that should have been recorded inside the material and was not made automatic mode never authenticate, and cost a hunt for a one-line defect.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: user_credentials and project_git_connections gain a nullable key_id text, and EncryptedSecret gains keyId?: string | null. Both tables change TOGETHER: they share the same envelope and the same script, and touching only one would produce a body of data in which the query answers half. A column, and not a prefix inside the blob, because the main consumer is an SQL query — step 2 of the runbook. A prefix would require reading and decoding each row to answer "how many are left", which is the question that motivated everything.
documents.s: 1. The envelope now carries key_id, in a COLUMN

documents.t: key_id = HMAC-SHA256(chave_derivada, 'brabo-master-key-id') → 16 primeiros hex This answers the TODO(humano) the activity left open — "where does the value of key_id come from? It cannot be a hash of the key (it gives an offline verification oracle to whoever reads the database), and a manual counter in the .env is one more variable the operator can get wrong." Both halves of the objection were addressed, and the first was measured, not assumed: There is no new oracle. Whoever reads the database already has a PERFECT offline verification oracle, and it is the envelope itself: wrapped_dek + dek_iv + dek_auth_tag are AES-256-GCM, which AUTHENTICATES. Testing a candidate passphrase is already today scryptSync(candidata, SALT, 32) followed by a decipher whose tag verifies or not — a right answer, per candidate. With key_id, testing the same candidate is scryptSync(candidata, SALT, 32) followed by an HMAC. The cost per attempt is the same in both cases, and it is dominated by scrypt, which both need to pay. An attacker with read access to the database gains nothing; what they would gain is something they already had. And there is no new variable. The operator does not type the key_id anywhere: it is a pure function of the key the operator already published. There is no second value to keep in sync, which was the argument the service's docblock used for not recording any id (envelope-encryption.service.ts:36-38, "um identificador de chave no registro é mais um metadado a manter em sincronia") — true for an ARBITRARY id, false for a fingerprint. What is recorded is an HMAC, not the key nor material from it, and it is 8 bytes.
documents.s: 2. The value is the FINGERPRINT of the derived key, and nothing more

documents.t: The read does NOT start choosing the key by the label. decrypt stays byte for byte as it is: try the current one, fall back to the previous one, GCM decides. rewrap also keeps the attempt as the criterion of "already on the current key". The obvious path — using key_id to skip the attempt — was considered and rejected for a failure mode of its own: a row whose label says "current" but whose envelope is on the old key would be skipped by rewrap silently, would be left out of the count of rewrapped ones, and step 3 of the runbook would make it illegible forever. The label is one more piece of data in a column; the envelope is the truth. Swapping cryptography's authority for a label turns a metadata inconsistency into secret loss. So the label serves three things, all outside the cryptographic decision path: the query of step 2 (WHERE key_id IS DISTINCT FROM '<atual>'); the diagnosis when NEITHER of the two keys opens — the message now names which key wrapped that record, distinguishing "came from another environment" from "record without key_id, written before this change" and from "the label says it is on the current one and it still does not open", which is the inconsistency above and deserves to be said out loud; the origin, which rewrap records together with the new envelope.
documents.s: 3. key_id is OBSERVABILITY, never AUTHORITY — and this is where this decision departs from the obvious

documents.t: key_id is born on the next write: encrypt records it, rewrap records it. Today's rows stay NULL, and NULL means exactly "written before this change, unknown key" — never "on the current key". Forcing a rewrap of the whole body of data only to fill the column would turn an observability improvement into a risky operation over every credential. Accepted and declared consequence: in an existing installation, the step 2 query only becomes valid after the first rotation. Before it, everything is NULL, and the honest answer of the query is "I know of none", which is different from zero — that is why the runbook's query counts the three bands separately (current / previous / unlabeled) instead of a single number.
documents.s: 4. No migration of the existing data

documents.t: A column nobody can compare against anything is useless. The service now logs at boot, in ONE line, the fingerprint of the current key, and the rotation warning that already existed (:75-78) now names BOTH. It is the same place the runbook already tells the operator to look ("Confirm the api is in rotation mode — it warns in the log"). Coming out in the log is safe by the same argument as point 2: it is an 8-byte HMAC, and it cheapens no attempt against the database.
documents.s: 5. The operator needs to know the CURRENT fingerprint, so the api says it

documents.t: What becomes possible Answering "how many credentials are still on the previous key?" in SQL, and that is what closes the criterion of BRB-016. The runbook uses the query in steps 2 and 3. Distinguishing, in the output of rewrap-deks.ts, a record from another environment from a tampered record — before they were the same error line. Interrupting step 2 and resuming knowing what is left, without depending on the count printed by an execution that has already ended. The price, declared A migration on two tables (ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN key_id text). Nullable and with no default, so it is new metadata in a new column: it does not rewrite rows, it does not lock a large table. The existing data stays unlabeled until the first rotation (point 4). An installation that restores a dump from ANOTHER environment gains a new and better symptom: the rows' key_id does not match the log's, and Restore no longer needs the diagnosis by elimination the runbook describes today. What does NOT change, and it is the half that matters The algorithm, the DEK size, the SALT and scrypt. No byte of encryptedApiKey is rewritten by any of this. decrypt. The two-key fallback remains the mechanism, and cryptography remains what decides. The script's name and invocation (node scripts/rewrap-deks.js), which the runbook already points to. The number of rotation steps: still three. This decision makes it OBSERVABLE, never shorter. What stays out, by name KMS, HSM and a per-tenant key remain another design, and ADR 0027 stays as it is. An index on key_id. The two tables are small by nature (one row per user/provider, one per project), and the query runs once every many months, in a rotation: an index would cost writes every day to save a seq scan twice a year. The decrypt half of the diagnosis. Whoever reads the diagnosis is the operator running the script, and that is where they are; putting the same message on the hot read path would change decrypt, which this ADR decided not to touch.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. It REVISES a decision declared in writing in docs/explanation/cadeia-de-suprimentos-do-ci.md — "pinning by tag is a deliberate stop, not an oversight" — and revokes it with measurement. It does not touch ADR 0119, which remains the owner of the four images the product publishes. It corresponds to BRB-004, a P2 of the maintainer's register.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: ADR 0119 made the four OWN images go by digest, and #419 gave the repository a mechanism for the other side of the same family: scripts/ci/actions-pinadas.ts, which fails a uses: pinned to a tag. Its docblock states the argument: Tag é um ponteiro que o dono da action pode remover e recriar apontando para outro commit (…). Quem move a tag executa código no runner que tem o checkout e, nos workflows de release, as credenciais do GHCR e do npm. That argument was never applied to image:, and the supply chain page said why: Third-party images are pinned by tag, not by digest (…) so this is weaker than the action pins — a deliberate stop, not an oversight. It buys the reproducibility that matters day to day (…) without the maintenance cost of digests on images we don't publish. The sentence has two premises, and measurement knocks down both. "Images we don't publish". Measured on 2026-09-12: there are 37 third-party references, and three of the places where they run are not "day to day". Thirteen are Dockerfile FROMs — node:24.11.1-alpine3.21, hexpm/elixir:1.17.3-…, nginx:1.27.5-alpine, alpine:3.20/3.20.3, node:24-alpine. Those are the base of the images we publish: third-party bytes we sign with cosign (RN-524) and deliver to other people. The alpine:3.20 of docker/backup/Dockerfile.prod is, by the way, the only FROM that BRB-004 itself already named. Four are in docker/docker-compose.install.yml, which is what comes up on the machine of whoever installed the product, next to that person's Postgres (RN-527). In the same file, the four own images arrive through a variable already resolved by digest, and the third-party ones arrived by tag. Four are in .github/workflows/ci.yml and golden-set-rag.yml, as job services:. That is literally the runner the actions rule exists to protect, reached through the other door — and neither of the two files had been looked at in that light. BRB-004 did not enumerate them either. "Maintenance cost". It is real and does not go away, but it is the SAME cost the repository already accepted for actions, whose pin is also moved by hand. What it buys is the same thing: referring to content, and not to a name someone else controls. There is also a trap recorded in writing in docs/reference/brb.md, and it explains why the item stayed open so long: read by its id, BRB-004 looks like the pinning of ollama:latest that PRs #401/#419 closed. "An id is not a description" — those PRs swapped latest for a version; this one asks for a digest.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: 1. Every third-party image is pinned by digest, with the tag in a comment next to it — the same shape actions use: image: neo4j@sha256:22ec5cd0… # 5.26-community In a Dockerfile the comment goes on the line ABOVE: # 3.20 FROM alpine@sha256:d9e853e8… AS runtime The digest is the index one (manifest list), never that of a platform: pinning the linux/amd64 manifest would break linux-arm64 without warning. The comment is mandatory, for the same reason as with actions — sha256:22ec5cd0… tells nobody that it is Neo4j 5.26 —, and it is one token, with no space: it is what separates the tag from the PROSE that already lives above almost every FROM of this repository. The position in a Dockerfile is not taste, and it was learned by getting it wrong. The first version of this change wrote FROM alpine@sha256:… # 3.20, by symmetry with the compose. Docker's parser only recognizes # at the START of a line: that is not a commented FROM, it is a FROM with three arguments, and the build dies with FROM requires either one or three arguments. The finding has a second half worth more than the first — hadolint had passed on all five Dockerfiles. It has its own parser, and a linter agreeing is not the build agreeing; whoever failed it was the bake of the images job, in 27 seconds. The check inherited the lesson in TWO forms. It recognizes the comment at the end of the FROM only to be able to fail it — a pattern that simply did not match the wrong line would make the reference VANISH from the scan instead of turning red, trading an error for silence, which is the defect this check exists not to have. And, for the same reason, the YAML comment is captured whole and judged afterwards, instead of validated inside the pattern. 2. A SIBLING check, not an extension. scripts/ci/imagens-pinadas.ts runs in the lint job, next to actions-pinadas.ts, and fails three things: a mutable reference, a digest without the tag in a comment, and the same tag with two different digests in different files. They are two scripts and not one because they are two questions: uses: lives in workflow YAML with one syntax; an image lives in compose, in kustomize manifests and in Dockerfiles, with three others. A function that answers both answers both badly — it is the same reasoning docs/.docmap.yml already uses to separate politica-de-branches from checks-e-rulesets. The third reason exists because of a concrete promise: golden-set-rag.yml says in a comment that it runs the "MESMA versão pinada de docker/docker-compose.yml", because the golden-set floor is keyed by model and not by environment (ADR 0138). With a tag that was a promise; with a digest it becomes verifiable. 3. The check does NOT cover the images the product publishes, and the decision is deliberate, with three independent reasons: They are not third-party. There is no owner outside this repository who could move any pointer. It is impossible. brabo-api:prod is a LOCAL tag produced by docker compose build: the digest does not exist before the build and changes on every build. A literal there would be requiring the nonexistent. It would fight the mechanism that already resolves them. Where they cross a registry, ADR 0119 already puts them by digest — .release/images.json written by release.yml, applied by make imagens-do-release. The overlay keeps the MARKER (REPLACE_WITH_DIGEST) and not a frozen release, on purpose: the repository does not declare that production runs v3.2.0. A check requiring a literal digest in the overlay would fail precisely the correct state. For the same reasons, interpolated references (${BRABO_API_IMAGE:?…}) stay out — install.sh writes the four into the .env already by digest — as do multi-stage stages (FROM deps AS build, FROM scratch), which are not registry images. The exception list is by name and fails closed: a new third-party image never matches brabo-, so it is born checked. 4. The observability compose enters, and that was an open question in the activity (TODO(humano): does it enter the check's scope, or stay out for not coming up in a user installation?). The answer is the cost of each side. Including it costs four digests. Excluding it costs a named exception inside docker/, which is exactly the shape of hole the docblock of actions-pinadas.ts diagnoses: "a new workflow is born copying its neighbor, and the neighbor was on a tag". An exempt file in the middle of the folder is the wrong neighbor.
documents.s: Decision

documents.t: The digest freezes, and the price is declared. An image pinned by digest does not receive a security fix until someone swaps the digest by hand — the same debt the actions' SHAs carry (BRB-006). This ADR does not solve that: it declares it. .github/dependabot.yml turns on the github-actions ecosystem for that reason; the docker ecosystem is not turned on here, and turning it on is a separate decision, because it changes the PR cadence of a monorepo that already turned off npm version updates due to flooding. Dev images freeze more than production ones. node:24-alpine was a rolling tag on purpose, and the digest pins it to a specific 24.x. It is the least comfortable consequence of this decision, and it is accepted by the same argument: the broker's dev image runs pnpm install in the build, and a base that changes underneath is one more variable when something breaks only on someone's machine. 37 lines changed and none changed content. Each digest was resolved against the registry from the tag that was already written, and it is the index digest — builds remain multi-arch. What the repository lost was the ability to receive different content without anyone seeing. BRB-004 stops reproducing, and formally closing it remains the job of whoever raised it, in the vault — the rule docs/reference/brb.md already states. What this ADR does NOT do: It does not extend to signatures. A digest is the integrity of what was pulled; provenance is BRB-005, whose open half (the proxy verifying the manifest's signature) was measured and rejected with a number (RN-525). It does not cover deploy/k8s/helm/otel-collector-values.yaml, where image: opens a map with repository: and no tag: whoever chooses the tag there is the chart, and pinning would require deciding the chart's version too. It stays DECLARED, not covered. It does not create an RN. The rule is a sibling of the one that forbids uses: by tag, and that one has no RN either: both live in CLAUDE.md (CI/CD release section) and in docs/explanation/cadeia-de-suprimentos-do-ci.md, which docs/.docmap.yml watches in block. Putting one of the two in docs/business-rules.md would give two addresses to the same policy.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-13 (AT-026). It extends ADR 0149 — the signed checksums.txt now covers more than binaries — and closes a gap of ADR 0150, which designed the one-line installer without saying how the installation compose would reach the installer's machine. Neither is edited; this document references them.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: The installer's E2E on a clean machine ran for the first time in session 8 of PHASE 30 (RN-549) and answered no to the question it existed to answer. install.sh brought up the stack with docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.install.yml — a path relative to the directory it ran from — used in seven places, including the up -d --wait. That file: was not a Release asset; was not in the signed checksums.txt; was downloaded nowhere — the script's only downloads were cosign, the manifest and its signature, images.json and the runner binary. And the compose bind-mounts two files relative to it: ./postgres/init.sql (the postgres one, which creates the pgvector extension) and ./ollama/pull-models.sh (the ollama-model-loader one, under the llm profile). The workaround step of install-e2e.yml brought exactly those three from the tag, through raw.githubusercontent.com. The symptom was late, and that is what made it expensive. Whoever followed the runbook's one-liner in an empty folder died with "no such file or directory" after the script had verified its own signature, detected the machine, asked for the base and written the .env with the five secrets. Half an installation, and a message that did not say what to do. Measured while implementing: there are four, not three. The MIGRATION path (migrar_instalacao_anterior, RN-530) runs bash docker/backup/test-restore-compose.sh — another relative path, and a script executed on the host. The E2E never reached it because on a clean machine there is nothing to migrate, and so the workaround did not bring it. In a folder without a checkout the migration would die there — before deleting anything, by construction of RN-530, but it would die. No layer below the E2E could see this: each piece worked and had its own suite. The defect was between the published artifact and the installer's machine, which is the boundary only the E2E crosses — and it only runs on a tag.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: 1. The files become Release assets and enter the SAME signed checksums.txt. Four, with names that do not collide: asset in the Release path in the repository and under the installation folder why brabo-install-compose.yml docker/docker-compose.install.yml the compose that brings up the installation brabo-install-postgres-init.sql docker/postgres/init.sql bind-mounted by postgres brabo-install-ollama-pull-models.sh docker/ollama/pull-models.sh bind-mounted by ollama-model-loader brabo-install-backup-test-restore.sh docker/backup/test-restore-compose.sh the migration's restore proof The Release is flat — an asset is a name, with no folder — and the manifest is indexed by name. init.sql and pull-models.sh are generic enough to collide with the next asset someone attaches, and two files with the same name would be a single line, with one's verification passing against the other's hash. Hence the brabo-install- prefix, which also does not match the --pattern 'brabo-runner-*' with which the checksums job downloads the binaries. The table lives in scripts/ci/assets-do-instalador.ts (who PUBLISHES) and in the case of destino_do_asset_do_instalador in install.sh (who DOWNLOADS). There are two because the installer runs with bash 3.2 on macOS and without Node; divergence is failed by assets-do-instalador.spec.ts, which reads the shell's case. The same spec DERIVES from the compose every ./… bind-mount and fails what is not in the table — which is exactly how the defect was born: someone added a mount and nobody asked how it would travel. 2. Whoever publishes is the checksums job of build-runner-binaries.yml, the same one that already publishes install.sh: the files come from the tag's checkout (the same commit that produced everything else signed there), are copied under the asset's name by the script, enter the sha256sum that generates the manifest and are attached together. Nothing changes in the wait for assets of RN-565: these do not come from the matrix, so there is nothing to wait for. The job now also checks each line of the manifest against the file (sha256sum -c --strict) after verifying the signature and before attaching — the signature proves who wrote the manifest; the check proves that what is going to be attached is what it says. 3. install.sh downloads and verifies the four BEFORE asking or writing anything. Right after verificar_a_si_mesmo, and against the SAME checksums.txt that function already verified (never a second download, for the reason it writes). The comparison is by exact field equality (awk), not by pattern: the name has dots. Three named and distinct refusals, because they call for different actions — the Release does not publish the asset (it predates this ADR, or came out half done), the manifest does not cover it, the hash does not match (incident). All say "Nada foi gravado", and it is true: up to there only a temporary directory was written to. 4. It never falls back to the relative path. COMPOSE_DE_INSTALACAO stops being the constant 'docker/docker-compose.install.yml' and is born empty; it only gets a value — an absolute path — when materializar_os_arquivos_da_instalacao copies the verified copies to <pasta de onde o script roda>/docker/, the same folder as the .env. That happens at the first instant a file is needed (the migration, or the startup right after the .env), never before: the no-TTY path still writes nothing. Whatever is already at the destination is replaced, never read — in an update it is the previous version's compose —, with an rm before copying so a symlink does not take the write elsewhere. The layout under the folder is the same as before on purpose: the compose's relative bind-mounts keep resolving, the marker keeps recording the compose and the command the runbook gives the operator does not change. 5. The E2E inverts what it demands. The workaround step goes away; in its place comes the assertion that the job's folder starts without docker/ (it has no checkout), that without a TTY the installer verified the files and wrote none, and — in its own step, after the installation, so the token is not in the installer's environment — that the written files are byte for byte the ones the Release's manifest covers. install-e2e.spec.ts stops demanding "both halves" of the workaround and starts demanding that it not come back.
documents.s: Decision

documents.t: Cloning the repository at the tag. It would be a single file to maintain, always coherent with the tag — and it would trade the signature chain for trust in the git transport, adding a dependency the clean machine may not have. What brings up the installation would become the only thing, among what the installer uses, that is not verified the way the binary is. A tarball with the four. One more file to extract on other people's machines, and a manifest line that covers four files without naming them — the same reason ADR 0149 preferred a manifest to five signatures, applied in reverse. Embedding the files in install.sh (heredoc). The compose has hundreds of lines and changes with the topology; the installer would change along with every service, and composes-em-conformidade.spec.ts would have to read shell. A variable or flag to point to another Release URL, for testing. It is the shortest form of a skip-verification door (ADR 0150). The shell tests pass the URL as the function's ARGUMENT, which is what main also does. Running install-e2e.yml on pull_request. It stays out, for the reason of ADR 0150.
documents.s: What this ADR explicitly rejects

documents.t: Closed in code, proven only at the next final tag. The pipeline only publishes on a tag and the E2E only runs after it; on a PR the static part runs (assets-do-instalador.spec.ts, install-e2e.spec.ts) and the functional shell part against a fake Release (install-arquivos-da-instalacao.spec.ts). Until the first tag after this merge, no published Release has the assets. No operator action, and no installation that worked stops working. The new install.sh only reaches someone inside a Release, and it is the SAME step of the SAME job that attaches it and attaches the four assets — so a Release with the new installer and without the files only exists if that step fails midway, and then the installer refuses early, with "a Release não publica …", instead of dying after the .env. Running the new install.sh from a checkout against an old Release was already refused before, by the origin verification (RN-526): its hash is not in the old manifest. Already published Releases keep the old installer and the workaround of running it from inside a checkout at the tag. The Release grows by four assets (~29 KB) and the manifest by four lines, and the four files become versioned together with the installer: changing one of them changes what the next tag signs. Changing the TABLE requires changing both sides, and the spec fails if only one changes. A checkout whose folder is the installation's has its docker/ overwritten by the Release's copies. At the tag being installed they are identical; outside it, git status gets dirty, and the script SAYS which ones it replaced. It is the price of the layout not changing, and it only exists for whoever installs from inside a checkout. The GET /runner-releases/binary proxy does not change: it reads the manifest as a name → hash map (RN-525), and extra lines do not affect it. Adjacency measured and NOT fixed. The migration's restore proof (test-restore-compose.sh) calls docker compose -f <compose> without --env-file, and Compose looks for the .env in the COMPOSE's folder, not the one it runs from (measured: docker compose -f docker/c.yml config with a .env only in the current directory fails interpolation). Since the compose lives in docker/ and the .env in the folder above, the BRABO_BACKUP_IMAGE variable does not arrive, and the proof tends to fail — a SAFE outcome by RN-530 (nothing is deleted), but migration by compose does not close. It is a pre-existing defect of the migration path, which no E2E exercises; it is declared here for the front that exercises it.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-18 (AT-085), with the answer "both" to the question "does the installer turn on the broker, or does the screen stop offering what does not run?". It revises the preselection of RN-513 (ADR 0146, point 4) and adds a local refusal reason to RN-521. Neither is edited; this document references them. Only the SCREEN half was delivered — the installer half was measured and stopped, for the reason in the section "The half that stopped".
documents.s: Status

documents.t: A real installation of v6.1.0, done through the one-liner on 2026-09-14, created a project in mounted through the web. It was the preselected mode: install.sh always writes BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE (the consented base, RN-531), and with a known base RN-513 preselects mounted. What followed in the event log: 6× dev.started → 6× dev.blocked_by_container; 2× container.start_failed with "BROKER_URL não está definida — o broker de container não faz parte desta instalação…". Nobody works on that project, ever. container and mounted only bring up a container through the BROKER (ADR 0144), and without a running container no dev agent command runs (ADR 0143). Only runner does not depend on it: whoever brings up the container is the local agent, on the user's machine (ADR 0137). And the /containers page let two container_start that could only fail be approved. Measured, and different from the activity's description: the installation compose did not "inherit the broker under a disabled profile". The broker service does not exist in docker/docker-compose.install.yml — its header says so at point 3 —, and the absence was decided in writing in decision 7 of ADR 0150, which also declared it "in the installer's output". The defect is not the installer hiding the absence: it is the SCREEN not knowing about it, and offering — even preselecting — the mode the absence makes useless.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: The maintainer's decision had a part (a): install.sh asking whether to turn on the broker, with the risk stated in text (the Docker socket mounted in a service is root-equivalent on the host). Before writing the question, it was measured whether the installation can have the image the "yes" answer would bring up. It cannot: docker-bake.hcl has four targets (api, engine, web, backup); scripts/ci/images-manifest.ts does not know broker; and the images.json of the v6.1.0 Release lists exactly those four; docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/daneiel/brabo-broker:6.1.0 answers denied (the repository does not exist), while the SAME anonymous command for ghcr.io/daneiel/brabo-api:6.1.0 resolves — it is not a lack of credentials; the v6.1.0 Release assets do not bring docker/broker/Dockerfile.prod nor the code of apps/broker/packages/docker-port, so a one-liner installation, which runs in a folder without a checkout (ADR 0160), does not even have anything to build. A question whose "yes" has no image to bring up is worse than none: the person consents to the socket risk and receives a pull access denied. Only --source=local (clean checkout, on a tag) could build the broker — and even there the installation compose does not have the service. The fix is the one ADR 0150 already named as small and outside its scope: publish the broker as a fifth image (a target in the bake, an id in the manifest, one more signature), and ONLY THEN the installer's question. It is left for its own front, and it is that front that reopens this half. install.sh was not touched by this ADR.
documents.s: The half that stopped: the installer cannot obtain the broker image

documents.t: brokerConfigurado: boolean enters two existing responses and no new route: GET workspaces/:workspaceId/projects-base — the creation wizard's question was already "which mode can this INSTALLATION execute?", and the base was only half of it. Same minimum (maintainer), same caller, same instant; GET workspaces/:workspaceId/containers — per ROW, with the same value in all. The response is a list, and swapping it for an envelope would break the contract for a field that belongs to the installation. The source is ContainerBrokerPort.configurado(), the SAME one that decides whether the observed-state read asks the broker or declares absence — reading BROKER_URL a second time would be the second source that one day diverges. The field says the variable EXISTS, never that the broker ANSWERS: whoever knows that remains naoObservado (RN-486).
documents.s: 1. The api says whether the installation has a broker, in the two routes the screen already reads

documents.t: Three states, which do not collapse: confirmed broker (true): RN-513 behavior intact — with a base, mounted preselected; confirmed absence (false): container and mounted stay ON THE SCREEN (removing the card would hide the information — the rule "remove the control, never the information" of RN-102) but inert, the reason is stated ONCE in text below them, and runner is the preselected one. A human choice made before the answer arrives, in a mode it makes unexecutable, falls back to runner — the same rule that already dropped mounted when the base disappears; don't know (loading, failing query, absent field): neither "has" nor "does not have". It does not preselect mounted — the revision of RN-513 —, and it also does not lock cards nor assert in text an absence nobody confirmed: container stays selected, as before.
documents.s: 2. The wizard does not preselect mounted without a broker, and offers runner

documents.t: decidirSubida gains the reason sem_broker_na_instalacao, for container and mounted when brokerConfigurado !== true — "don't know" does not become "has". It comes right after ja_esta_de_pe and BEFORE sem_imagem_decidida: in an installation with nobody to bring up the container, sending someone to decide the image would be pointing to the wrong door. runner never falls into it. The branching is the same by DESTINATION as acaoDeSubidaDoModo (whoever depends on the broker is whoever proposes container_start), read on the other side by usaBroker, and not a second rule.
documents.s: 3. /containers refuses the startup before the click, with its own reason

documents.t: In a Release installation, the mode that works end to end becomes the suggested one, and the one that does not work starts saying why before anyone chooses it. The price: runner requires the local agent up and Docker on the user's machine — which the one-liner installation already delivers (ADR 0155). In the DEVELOPMENT compose the broker comes up by default (RN-512), but BROKER_URL stays empty until someone puts it in the .env (docker/docker-compose.yml, .env.example). Without it, the developer's wizard now shows the warning — and it is RIGHT: without BROKER_URL, the api never calls the broker that is up, and container_start would fail the same way. RN-512 does NOT change: the broker remains under profiles: ["container-broker"] in the production compose, outside the installation compose, and none of the five containment layers is touched. What changes is the SCREEN stopping assuming the opposite. Out of scope, declared: the installer half (section above) — it depends on publishing the image; mode conversion (ExecutionModeSection, ADR 0111) can still convert to container/mounted in an installation without a broker; it reads the same route and the field is at hand, but it is another screen, with another offering rule (RN-559); stopping and removing (container_stop/container_remove) did not gain the refusal: without a broker there is no container/mounted container registered as up to stop, and the case was not measured; the Infra Lead does not know about an absent broker — it refuses by MODE (RN-566), and enriching its context with the installation is the more expensive front RN-566 already declares; the parallelization suggestion that ignores an agent blocked by a container; the closing sentence of install.sh says that without a broker "a project in Mounted folder mode does not bring up a container" and omits the container mode, which does not either — an adjacency measured and not fixed here, because the installer belongs to another parallel front.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-18 (AT-097). It closes decision 7 of ADR 0150 ("the broker does not come up in this phase, and the consequence is stated"), extends ADR 0119 from four to five images and applies to the installation the argument that ADR 0146 (RN-512) applied to the development compose. The broker itself — the five layers, the five operations, the computed spec — is that of ADR 0130, and nothing in it changes. None of these is edited; this document references them. Sibling: ADR 0161 delivered the WEB half of the same maintainer decision ("both") — project creation only offers the mode the installation executes — and declared in writing that the INSTALLER half stopped because the image was not published. This ADR is that half. The two complete each other without depending on each other: that one prevents the screen from offering what the installation does not execute; this one gives the installation a way to execute, with consent. With the broker on, the installation gets BROKER_URL, and it is through it that 0161's screen offers both modes again.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: In a real installation, a container or mounted project never executes. Whoever brings up the container of those two modes is the broker (ADR 0144 branches by DESTINATION: container and mounted → broker), and the installation compose does not have the service. BROKER_URL stays undefined, container_start ends in container.start_failed with BrokerIndisponivelError, and the dev agents stay in dev.blocked_by_container forever — RN-502 refuses, rightly, to execute outside a running container. Decision 7 of ADR 0150 declared this and called the fix small. Measured on 2026-09-18, when opening this front: docker manifest inspect ghcr.io/daneiel/brabo-broker:6.1.0 → denied; the same question for brabo-api:6.1.0 resolves. The image does not exist in the registry. docker-bake.hcl had four targets (api, engine, web, backup), and scripts/ci/images-manifest.ts accepted exactly the four. docker/broker/Dockerfile.prod already existed, and already went through ci.yml's hadolint together with the other four — FROM by digest with the tag on the line above, USER node, HEALTHCHECK against /health, npm/corepack removed. What was missing was not the image: it was someone building, scanning and publishing it. ci.yml never built it; docker-compose.prod.yml referenced it as brabo-broker:prod, which only existed on the machine of whoever ran docker compose build with the profile. The Release does not bring the code, so --source=local — the path ADR 0150 pointed to as the way out — requires a checkout on a tag, which is not the one-line installation.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: A broker target in docker-bake.hcl, inside the default group: ci.yml now builds it on every PR, checks that it does not run as root, scans it in Trivy with the same rules (HIGH,CRITICAL, --ignore-unfixed) and proves it COMES UP healthy with a read-only rootfs. release.yml publishes it by DIGEST, images-manifest.ts requires it (a missing target still fails — five of five or none), and keyless cosign signing and the verification in the same run (RN-524) cover it without a new line, because both loops read the manifest. Kubernetes does not know it, and that is a decision, not forgetfulness: there is no broker Deployment in deploy/k8s/, and mounting a node's socket into a pod is another privilege conversation. argumentosDeSetImage now emits only the images the kustomize base declares — make imagens-do-release keeps writing four lines into the overlay.
documents.s: 1. The broker is the FIFTH published image, with the same gates as the others

documents.t: The service enters under profiles: ["container-broker"], the SAME profile as the validation compose, and with the five layers of ADR 0130 intact: no ports:, only on the broker network (internal: true, which only the api reaches and which has no egress), BRABO_SERVICE_TOKEN mandatory in production, five operations, a spec computed from what the api says. The socket is mounted in it and in no other. api now always participates in the broker network — as it already does in the validation compose —, and BROKER_URL in the api stays empty unless the .env says otherwise. The image comes from BRABO_BROKER_IMAGE, mandatory like the other four, and that was measured and not chosen: Compose interpolates the WHOLE file before filtering by profile, so a ${VAR:?…} in a disabled service refuses the file all the same. The installer always writes it (it comes from the same manifest), whether it turns on the broker or not. The two roots go as in the validation compose: BRABO_PROJECTS_HOST_BASE derives from BRABO_PROJECTS_BASE, which is already a host path. The other, PROJECT_WORKSPACES_HOST_ROOT, has no way to derive in the compose — the installation's managed folder is the NAMED volume project_workspaces, and the path the daemon resolves is the HOST's. The installer COMPUTES it (<DockerRootDir>/volumes/brabo_project_workspaces/_data, the local driver's layout) and, after startup, CHECKS it against the Mountpoint the daemon returns for the volume; diverging becomes a named pending item with the right value, never a silently guessed value.
documents.s: 2. The installation compose gains the service, OFF by default

documents.t: A new question, after the base and before the .env. It says what turning it on grants — a service of this installation starts talking to this machine's Docker, and whoever commands that service commands Docker —, what the layers contain, and what changes without it (container and mounted projects do not execute; the Runner mode does not depend on it). Only s/sim turns it on. Enter, anything else or the lack of a terminal leave it off, and the script SAYS it stayed off. Yes writes into the .env COMPOSE_PROFILES=container-broker, BROKER_URL=http://broker:8090, the DOCKER_GID and the computed root. The DOCKER_GID is measured from inside a container, with the broker image itself and the socket mounted through --mount type=bind (which refuses instead of creating the folder when the source does not exist), because it is the gid the process sees there that group_add needs — and on Docker Desktop the socket's gid on the host says nothing about the one inside the VM. Not being able to measure, or the path not being a socket, is a NAMED refusal that teaches to run again and answer no; never a guessed 999. The decision appears in the final summary, and the sentence "what this installer does NOT do" stops saying that only "Mounted folder" stays without a container: container does too.
documents.s: 3. The installer ASKS, with the risk stated in text, and the default is NO

documents.t: ADR 0146 separated the two composes by what the socket MEANS: in development whoever brings up the stack already has the socket, so the broker receiving it grants nothing the operator does not have; in production the socket is a privilege boundary and the operator is not the developer. The one-line installation is the first case, not the second. It runs on the person's own machine, who just ran docker compose up — the installer does not work without them having the socket. Operator and user are the same person. What the installation CANNOT assume, and that is why it asks instead of turning it on like the development compose, is that whoever installs knows what the socket is: the dev compose is read by whoever develops the product; the installer is run by whoever never opened this repository. Explicit consent is the difference that remains, and it is the one this ADR buys. docker-compose.prod.yml does not change: it remains under a profile, and for it ADR 0146's reading still holds without caveat.
documents.s: 4. Why RN-512's argument holds here

documents.t: The price, declared. A root-equivalent image becomes public. Anyone can pull ghcr.io/daneiel/brabo-broker. The image itself grants nothing — it is the mounted socket that grants —, but it becomes a studiable target, and a vulnerability in it becomes, in every installation that turned it on, a path to the host's Docker. That is why it enters each PR's Trivy and each tag's signature, and not a separate list. The Docker socket is now mounted in a service of a user installation, when it consents. Whoever commands the broker commands the machine's Docker. What separates it from the rest: it publishes no port, only the api reaches it, the token is compared in constant time, and there is no field where one could write privileged, cap_add, network: host or a free -v. That contains the caller; it does not contain a bug in the broker itself. BRABO_BROKER_IMAGE becomes mandatory in the installation's .env, on or not. A .env written by a previous installer does not have it — but the installer rewrites the .env on every execution, and the update goes through it. The installer requires broker in images.json. A Release prior to this one does not have it, and this version's installer refuses naming the target. It is the same rule as ADR 0160: a tag's installer installs that tag. The managed root depends on the local driver's layout. Computed before startup, checked after; what does not check out becomes a pending item with the value read from the daemon. Not measured: the DOCKER_GID and the computed root on macOS Docker Desktop. The tag's E2E runs the interactive half only on Linux. What does NOT change. The validation compose, smoke.sh (which comes up without the profile and keeps proving the same three app images), the development compose, Kubernetes, and the broker itself.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. 2026-09-18 (AT-089). It generalizes the breaking of the synchronous block that ADR 0086 did only for the suspended Dev Lead. ADR 0086 is not edited: what it decided (the turn that SUSPENDS answers the from right away and emits agent.status: awaiting_approval instead of agent.done) remains valid — this document only moves the answer's moment earlier for EVERY turn, and with that its case stops being the only one. Rule: RN-578.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: In a real v6.1.0 installation (09/14), three clicks hung for the ENTIRE turn of the agent they triggered: api route request time POST …/agents/criativo/structured-question/:id/answer 97.3 s POST …/sessions/:id/readiness 97.3 s POST …/agents/arquiteto/handoff-infra 51.8 s The event log of the same session matches all three to the tenth of a second (from the user's event to the agent's persisted agent.status: idle): 97.2 s, 97.3 s and 51.7 s. The reason is a single one: every user route that talks to a conversational agent goes through EngineWeb.AgentCommandController, which does a synchronous GenServer.call (120 s on the Criativo (Creative), 180 s on the others) — and the agent's handle_call, since RN-122, deferred the answer until the turn's Task ended (TurnoAssincrono.iniciar/3 kept the from and answered in tratar_resultado/2). The controller already returned 202 and already discarded the return ("esta resposta é só o aceite"), and the OpenAPI of …/message already said "the response is just the acknowledgment". The acknowledgment only arrived at the end of the turn. Three consequences, all measured: The button "does not respond". For the person, a click that takes 97 s is a click that failed. A turn above the ceiling becomes an error in a command that worked. The GenServer.call exits by :timeout in the controller's process, Phoenix returns 500, the api becomes 500, and the screen shows an error — while the turn keeps running and ends successfully. The kickoffs of the same session (which are cast, and therefore do not suffer) lasted 7.5 min (PO), 6.6 min (Arquiteto) and 8.4 min (Infra): a turn above 120 s is not a hypothesis. Silent refusal. A message that arrives with a turn already running receives {:error, :turno_em_andamento}, which the controller discarded and answered 202. In the same session, a "Continue" typed 2.5 min into the Arquiteto's kickoff was accepted successfully and never read — no agent.status: working after it, no agent.error. Worse: the screen left the composer free during that kickoff (the accepted handoff arms the strip without streaming), so it was the natural path.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: TurnoAssincrono.iniciar/3 answers the from ON ACCEPTING. With the Task up and agent.status: working already persisted, handle_call returns {:reply, :ok, state}. The from stops traveling in state.turno_assincrono; tratar_resultado/2 and cancelar/1 no longer answer anyone. It is the SAME mechanism for the six conversational agents — no second path —, and ADR 0086 becomes a particular case: the suspended Dev Lead still has no agent.done, it is just no longer the only one to answer early. Only the wait leaves the request; the refusal stays in it. What the agent refuses BEFORE bringing up the Task remains synchronous, and now has its own status instead of the silent 202: turn already running → 409 (turno_em_andamento), and now with a durable agent.error (origin politica) saying the message was recorded and not read; Dev Lead with a pending plan in Approvals → 409 (aguardando_aprovacao, the agent.error that already existed); Criativo without a captured business rule → 422 (sem_regra_de_negocio, idem). The api passes those two statuses on as ConflictException / UnprocessableEntityException with the engine's sentence. Validation that was already synchronous in the api (409 for an already answered form, 400 for a missing answer, 400 of RN-160) does not move. The api's HTTP status does NOT change. The routes keep 201 { ok: true }. The body and status always meant "accepted" — what changed is WHEN it arrives. Switching to 202 would change the generated contract without changing any meaning, and the user's event (chat.message, readiness.confirmed, architecture.readiness_confirmed) is written before the answer, so the 201 remains true. The turn's failure remains durable, and only there. Everything that was already agent.error (crash, invalid format, cancellation, failure narrated by the api) still is, with the same origin. What disappears is its mirror in HTTP — which was never read: the controller discarded it. The screen follows the end through the channel, and the safety net changes signal. The web's four callers treated "the call resolved" as "the turn ended" (RN-131's safety net against a lost agent.done). That signal ceased to exist. In its place, acompanharTurnoPeloLog (in lib/session-turno.ts): while the strip is on, every 4 s it reads the tail of the event log and closes the turn when the MOST RECENT persisted agent.status of the agent in question is not working. It is reliable because of the ordering of item 1: the new turn's working is persisted BEFORE the acknowledgment, so an old idle is never the most recent after it. Offering the Dev Lead still comes AFTER the Arquiteto's closing turn. OfferInfraHandoffUseCase calls offerInfraHandoff and then offerDevHandoff, and the order of the two handoffs in the event log came from the wait. Without it, the Dev one would be born before the Infra one. ArquitetoServer now DEFERS the :offer_dev_handoff that arrives with a turn running and executes it when the turn closes — by success, failure, crash or cancellation, the same set of outcomes in which it was offered before.
documents.s: Decision

documents.t: The click's time becomes that of the acknowledgment (record the user's event + bring up the Task + persist working), and a long turn stops becoming a 500. The GenServer.call ceiling still exists, but now measures the handle_call, not the turn. A refusal that was silent becomes a visible error. Whoever types during a turn (including a kickoff) now sees 409 with the reason, and the thread gains the agent.error. The chat.message the api recorded BEFORE asking the engine remains in the log — orphaned as before, but now explained. Refusing before recording would require the api to ask the engine whether there is a turn, and the answer would age before the POST; it was not done. Story return (ReturnStoryUseCase) remains best-effort: a 409 there is logged and swallowed like any other failure to notify the PO — the refusal is already recorded. The difference is that the agent.error now exists. The screen's safety net costs one read of the log's tail every 4 s DURING the turn — a period in which the screen's 3 s poll is paused (findings 2/7). If the engine restarts in the middle of the turn, no idle arrives and the strip stays on until "Stop" (which closes locally) or a reload: before, the same scenario became a 500 on the click. Declared, not solved. A message to infra through the composer falls into the final clause of AgentCommandController.message/2, which routes to the Criativo. Pre-existing, measured here and NOT fixed — it is another front.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-18 (AT-092). It revises the TRIGGER of RN-522, which had been born to keep the promise of RN-541 ("the bootstrap is deferred until the Arquiteto's handoff"). Neither came from an ADR — both were born from a direct request of the product owner and live only in docs/business-rules.md —, so this is the first structural record of the moment the repository is born. The provisioning MECHANISM does not change: it is the same ProvisionRepositoryUseCase, idempotent by design since ADR 0005, called by the same AcceptHandoffUseCase. The handoff target rule of ADR 0038 (an external handoff addresses only an area lead or an agent without an area) and the Arquiteto → Dev Lead chain of ADR 0053 remain intact.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: A real v6.1.0 installation, on 2026-09-14, produced this sequence in the event log of a new project: 02:40:54 — the Arquiteto (Architect) proposes open_adr_pr three times. The repository does not exist yet, and the tool fails all three times. 02:43:53 — handoff.offered to infra and to dev-lead (the architecture readiness confirmation offers both, OfferInfraHandoffUseCase). Only the infra one is accepted. The dev-lead one stays offered. 03:02:34 — POST /projects/:id/execution/activate answers 201. project_repositories, project_git_connections and repo_bootstraps stay empty. The project stays without a repository forever. The two defects are independent, and RN-522 carried both: The trigger was after whoever needs the repository. The Arquiteto is the first agent with a tool that WRITES to the repository (open_adr_pr), and the Infra Lead, activated by the Arquiteto → Infra handoff, is the second (open_infra_pr). Both work BEFORE the acceptance to the Dev Lead. RN-541 said "the repository is born when development starts", and development, measured by what the agents do, starts at the Arquiteto. The only trigger was SKIPPABLE. Activating execution does not require an accepted handoff to the Dev Lead — it requires a current module_map, and nothing else. Whoever activates through the Overview (or through the "Activate execution" shortcut of the handoff card itself, RN-137) skips the acceptance, and with it the provisioning. Nothing on the path refused. Who hands off to the Arquiteto, measured. The Arquiteto can only be activated with an accepted handoff addressed to it (canActivateAgent, domain/sessions/agent-activation.ts) — the exception is only the Criativo (Creative). The handoff is born through two doors, and both write through the SAME CreateHandoffUseCase: the PO, when finishing the backlog, with offer_handoff(to_agent: "arquiteto") (the kickoff instruction in po_server.ex says so), or the user, through the manual handoff (RequestManualHandoffUseCase, ADR 0109). And the acceptance is a single one: AcceptHandoffUseCase, the same one that already hosted RN-522's trigger. There is no path in which the Arquiteto works without having gone through that acceptance.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: 1. The trigger becomes the acceptance of the handoff addressed to arquiteto. In AcceptHandoffUseCase, the branch that calls provisionarRepositorio now fires for toAgent === 'arquiteto', BEFORE activateAgent — the same order RN-522 already used, for the same reason: the Arquiteto wakes up in a project that already has somewhere to work, and the first open_adr_pr finds a repository. Everything else in the branch stays byte for byte: always local (the only provider without credentials), a failure becomes repository.provision_failed with an origin and never brings down the acceptance, an ADOPTED repository leaves early without being a failure. 2. The old trigger STAYS, as a second idempotent door. The acceptance to dev-lead keeps calling the same provisioning. Three reasons, in order of weight: It is the way out for the projects already broken. A project that went past the Arquiteto BEFORE this change (AT-092's exp001 is exactly that: handoff to the Arquiteto accepted under the old rule, handoff to the Dev Lead still offered) has a pending handoff whose acceptance provisions. Without this door, the only way out would be the manual provisioning page, which no screen offers from the session. It is the natural retry of a failure. If provisioning fails at the acceptance to the Arquiteto, the event stays in the log, and the next step the user takes anyway — accepting the Dev Lead — tries again, without anyone needing to know a provisioning route exists. The price is zero by construction. With the created repository already up, ProvisionRepositoryUseCase does not call createRepo, creates neither session nor bootstrap, and the runner reports all steps as satisfied (ADR 0005). That was already proven for three consecutive runs of the use case; what this ADR adds is the proof THROUGH BOTH DOORS: accepting the Arquiteto and then the Dev Lead, against real Postgres and LocalGitProvider, ends with ONE createRepo, ONE row in project_repositories, ONE in repo_bootstraps, and no repository.provision_failed. Removing the second door was considered and rejected: it has no cost, and the alternative leaves exp001 with no way out through the screen where the user is. 3. execution/activate without a repository is REFUSED with 409. In ActivateExecutionUseCase, right after the module_map check and BEFORE any effect (persisting budget, seeding permissions.json, creating a session), the use case queries ProvisionedRepositoryRepository.findByProjectId. Without a row, ConflictException with a NAMED reason, chosen by the state of the project's handoffs (HandoffRepository.findByProject, a new read and only a read) by a pure domain function: there is an offered handoff to the Arquiteto → "accept the handoff to the Arquiteto"; otherwise, there is an offered handoff to the Dev Lead → "accept the handoff to the Dev Lead" (the second door); otherwise, one of the two was already accepted → automatic provisioning ran and left no repository (repository.provision_failed says why), and the path is the project's provisioning page; otherwise → no handoff to the Arquiteto was accepted, and the repository is born there. An ADOPTED repository counts as a repository. 409 and not 400 because the request is right: it is the project's STATE that does not yet allow it. Reactivating an execution that is already running is still not a conflict WHEN there is a repository; exp001, which activated without having one, now also receives the 409 on reactivation — and that is what is wanted, because its dev agents never had anywhere to work. 4. The screen does not offer activating without a repository, and says why once, in text. The Overview's Execution section reads GET .../git/repository (the same queryKey ['repository', projectId] that ProjectPage, CodeShell and Settings already use — no truly new request) and, with a CONFIRMED null answer, leaves the button inert in place and writes the reason, with the link to the provisioning page. Loading or with an error, the button stays as it was: "don't know" does not become "doesn't have", and the backend refuses anyway. On the handoff card to the Dev Lead, inside the session, the "Activate execution" shortcut disappears while the repository does not exist, and the card says that accepting the handoff provisions it — the accept button is right next to it. It is the rule of RN-102 and ADR 0064: remove the control, never the information.
documents.s: Decision

documents.t: RN-522 changes trigger, not mechanism. RN-582 records the new rule; RN-522 and RN-541 gain a note pointing to it, and the creation wizard's comment stops saying "Dev Lead". The Arquiteto → Infra before Dev Lead case ceases to exist. The Infra Lead is activated by the Arquiteto's handoff, which by construction only exists after the acceptance to the Arquiteto — so the repository has already been born when it wakes up. The local refusal of open_adr_pr/open_infra_pr (AT-088) remains necessary, and complementary: it covers provisioning that FAILED and the legacy project, which this ADR cannot prevent from existing. A consequence measured in the code and accepted: the git-bootstrap session is now born in the MIDDLE of the Arquiteto's phase. ProvisionRepositoryUseCase opens its own session for the bootstrap log, and the Overview and the workspace summary choose the "most recent" session by createdAt. Under RN-522 that session was born at the acceptance to the Dev Lead and was soon overtaken by the execution one; now it becomes the project's "most recent" during the whole conversation with the Arquiteto, until the next session is born. The chat session is not affected (its screen reads its own id). Fixing it requires deciding whether the bootstrap log deserves its own session, or whether "the most recent" should ignore system sessions — both touch another front's rule (RN-139, ADR 0005), and are not decided here. A project with no handoff to the Arquiteto at all, with a module_map written outside the flow, falls into the refusal's fourth reason and leaves through the provisioning page. There is no automatic path for it, and there does not need to be. Rejected: provisioning at project creation (it would undo RN-541, which is the product owner's request); provisioning INSIDE execution/activate (activation would gain a hidden git effect, and the agents before it would remain without a repository — defect 1 entirely); and moving the trigger without keeping the old door (it would leave exp001 with no way out through the session).
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the maintainer on 2026-09-18 (AT-090): "the routing preference is CONFIGURABLE PER BINDING". It extends ADR 0041 (capability in two layers, only declared when proven) and ADR 0042 (what produced the number goes frozen in the token_usage row). It edits neither. The rule born from here is RN-583.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: Measured in the token_usage of the v6.1.0 installation (2026-09-14): 24 calls of ~deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-latest via openrouter. The upstream_provider (RN-042) already said who served each one: Relace in 23, with an average latency of 69.5 s (between 32 and 47 tok/s), and Baidu in 1, with 37.8 s (~190 tok/s). OpenRouter chooses the upstream through a balancing that favors PRICE when the request says nothing — and openrouter-provider.ts said nothing: the /chat/completions body went out without provider/sort. The hub accepts provider: { sort: "price" | "throughput" | "latency" } in the body. The remaining question is a PRODUCT one, not a wire one: who chooses the criterion, and where that choice lives.
documents.s: Context

documents.t: routing_preference (enum routing_preference: price | throughput | latency), nullable, in model_bindings. null is today's behavior: nothing is sent and the hub decides on its own. The column enters apps/api/src/db/schema/llm.ts, where the binding already lives — the aggregate is the model's, and the enum lives with the two tables that call it (the enum rule of ADR 0121).
documents.s: 1. A column in the binding, in the llm aggregate

documents.t: The cascade (session > agent > area > project > workspace, plus the Criativo's (Creative's) post-cascade step) remains a binding cascade. The winning binding brings the model AND its preference; no level "inherits only the preference" from another. Three reasons: The preference only makes sense together with the model with which it was chosen. It exists for ONE provider (the hub); cascading it separately would produce combinations nobody chose — the agent's model on a provider without the capability and the project's throughput, or the workspace's latency applied to a model the workspace owner never saw. An independent cascade would require a second chain on the screen. RN-470 made the MODEL's chain visible node by node; two chains landing at different levels on the same row would be exactly the state the screen does not know how to explain. The level the cascade SKIPS takes the preference with it. A binding skipped for unavailability or lack of tool calling stops being valid whole — model and criterion. Having only the criterion survive would be the same defect as the first reason, created by the fall. Written consequence: to put throughput on an entire area, one writes it on the AREA's binding; the agent that diverges with its own binding has ITS preference (null until someone chooses).
documents.s: 2. The preference does NOT cascade on its own: it travels with the binding that won

documents.t: PUT .../model-binding (all five scopes) gains routingPreference?: 'price' | 'throughput' | 'latency' | null: absent — preserves the recorded preference, if the new model's provider accepts it; otherwise it becomes null. Omitting cannot clear silently (that is how the usual model swap and "apply to all" keep calling the route), and it also cannot leave recorded a criterion the new provider does not understand; null — clears, explicitly; a value, with a provider without the capability — 422 (RoutingPreferenceNotSupportedError), in the same filter as the other binding refusals. The request is well formed; what does not hold is the combination. The invariant the three rules sustain: no binding keeps a preference for a provider that does not declare it.
documents.s: 3. The write: absent preserves, null clears, a provider without the capability refuses

documents.t: LLMProviderCapabilities.routingPreference, mandatory like embeddings (an optional field would be the new provider that forgets to declare). All nine declare it. The wire mapping (provider: { sort }) is an OpenRouter particularity and enters as a hook of its config (campoDeRoteamento), in the design of extrairUpstreamProvider: the base only calls it when the capability is true AND there is a preference — never if (name === 'openrouter') in the parsing. The MODEL layer gains no column: sort is a criterion of the HUB over the upstreams that serve the model, OpenRouter's catalog does not publish it per row, and a model with a single upstream receives it as a no-op. Inventing the column would be a capability without a source. OpenRouter's value is whatever the proof says. The capability only becomes true with the smoke against the real API (openrouter-provider.roteamento.smoke.spec.ts) returning the chosen upstream. Without a credential in the implementer's environment, it is born false and the feature is born DORMANT: the route refuses with 422 and the screen says in text that no provider of this installation has the option proven.
documents.s: 4. A PROVIDER capability, declared false while not proven

documents.t: token_usage.routing_preference, nullable, written per call: the preference that went over the wire — null when the binding had none, and null also when it had one but the provider does not declare it (it was not sent, so it is the provenance of nothing). It is the same rule as the frozen price: without it, comparing the upstream_provider and latency_ms of before and after turning on throughput would depend on reconstructing the state of the binding at that instant, which is recorded nowhere.
documents.s: 5. What was ASKED goes frozen in token_usage

documents.t: GET llm/provider-capabilities returns the capabilities of the nine providers, read from the registry's instances — the same source the adapter uses. A new route, and not a field in an existing response, because no existing response is about a PROVIDER: the model is a catalog row (the vendor's fact, MesmasChaves with the entity) and the binding is a scope's decision. No role (authentication only), like users/me/credentials: it is a fact of this installation's code, the same for everyone. The control lives where the binding is edited — the agents table and the areas section in Settings —, with the ENDPOINT's minimum role (RN-102): developer on the agent, maintainer on the area. It is only editable on the row that HAS its own binding; on the inheriting row, it says from which level the current criterion came. A model whose provider does not have the capability gains no option — it gains the sentence saying why.
documents.s: 6. The screen discovers the capability through a PROVIDER route

documents.t: With the capability true, putting throughput on an OpenRouter binding changes the body of every call that resolves to it, and the token_usage row says which criterion was asked and who served — the before/after comparison is a query, not a reconstruction. While the capability is false, nothing changes on the wire for anyone: the code is in place, the route refuses and the screen explains. Flipping the flag is a one-line PR accompanied by the smoke's output. Declared price: sort: throughput can route to a more EXPENSIVE upstream. Metering keeps charging the model's catalog price (ADR 0042), which is OpenRouter's reference price and not the upstream's — that difference already existed and is not measured here. Out of scope, declared: the session (SessionPage) and the project and workspace levels have no control on the screen: the API accepts the field in all five scopes, but project and workspace have no model selector on any screen (measured: no setProjectModelBinding/setWorkspaceModelBinding is called by the web), and the session selector is another surface; the agent card (Overview/Executors) shows the model and does NOT edit the binding — the control did not go there, because the binding is not edited there; the other fields of OpenRouter's provider object (order, only, ignore, allow_fallbacks, max_price) and the :nitro suffix: none was asked for, and each one is a product decision of its own.
documents.s: Consequences

documents.t: Accepted. Decided by the product owner on 2026-09-26 (AT-226), among three options: "with automatic mode on, the agent executes any terminal command without approval, including outside the project folder". It revises, ONLY for an agent in automatic mode, the path scope ceiling of ADR 0055. It edits neither 0055 nor ADR 0102 (the external effect/privileged command ceiling, RN-418), which remain valid in full. The rule born from here is RN-603; it revises RN-153 and RN-154.
documents.s: Status

documents.t: "Automatic mode" (RN-153) is the "*" wildcard in agent_autonomy: autonomy for any action type of an agent. It was designed NOT to break any ceiling of decide() — the ceilings acted on current.policy === 'auto_approve', without knowing where the permissiveness came from (RN-154). One of those ceilings is the PATH SCOPE one (ADR 0055): a terminal command that touches a path outside the project folder is never auto-approvable.
